solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Henry to appear with holdall — one to fix locks needed

blocks.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance
a programme that airs is broadcast, so it appears
a grip is an old word for a travelling bag

explanation.surface: Henry turns up with a big bag, and someone is needed to fix the locks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Locks' looks like door hardware; here it is a head of hair.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairgrip is a sprung clip used to hold strands of hair in place.

clue.text: Fabled woodcutter joins a party with a scholar

blocks.note: taken as written
LIB is short for the Liberal party
taken as written; with simply joins
a BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate

explanation.surface: A legendary woodcutter signs up to a party alongside an academic.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Arabian Nights tale, Ali Baba is a poor woodcutter who finds the forty thieves' treasure.

clue.text: Evidently embarrassed to be associated with growing relief organisation?

blocks.note: visibly embarrassed people go red in the face
crescent comes from Latin crescere, to grow, as of a waxing moon

explanation.surface: An aid agency is visibly ashamed to be linked with an expanding charity.
explanation.definitionFit: The Red Crescent is the Red Cross movement's emblem and name in Muslim countries, giving humanitarian relief.

clue.text: Amber for instance about to stray from path

blocks.note: re means about, concerning
to sin is to stray from the path of righteousness

explanation.surface: A traffic light on amber tempts a driver to wander off course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amber' looks like a traffic-light colour; it is fossilised tree gum.
explanation.definitionFit: Amber is fossilised resin from ancient trees, so it is an example of the substance.

clue.text: Depression grips woman climbing wondrous monument

indicators.note: something that grips holds another thing firmly inside it
in a down clue climbing means reading upwards, from bottom to top

blocks.note: a dip is a hollow in the ground
a common woman's name

explanation.surface: A woman climbs out of a hollow towards a marvellous monument.
explanation.definitionFit: The Great Pyramid of Giza is one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.

clue.text: Strut surely has broken inside for example

indicators.note: something broken is smashed apart, so the letters of has are rearranged
inside tells us the shuffled word sits within the phrase that follows

blocks.note: the letters of has, rearranged
say, as in 'take a fruit, say', introduces an example

explanation.surface: A strut, it is claimed, has given way inside, as an example of structural failure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strut' looks like a structural beam; 'surely' belongs with it, describing a confident walk.
explanation.definitionFit: To sashay is to walk with a showy, self-assured swing, which is strutting with confidence.

clue.text: Space flight takes one coming into sun source

indicators.note: coming into means entering, so one item is placed within the other

blocks.note: the sun is a star
I is the Roman numeral one
a well is a source of water

explanation.surface: A space mission carries one person flying towards the sun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Space flight' suggests a rocket; the flight is a flight of stairs, and the space is the shaft it occupies.
explanation.definitionFit: A stairwell is the vertical shaft in a building that a flight of stairs runs up.

clue.text: Runner on snow finally approaches Karakoram mountain

indicators.note: finally points to the end of the word, so only its closing letter is used

blocks.note: the closing letter of approaches
K1, also called Masherbrum, is a Karakoram peak; the numeral 1 is read as I

explanation.surface: A skier finally nears a peak in the Karakoram range.
explanation.walkthrough: Karakoram peaks were surveyed as K1, K2 and so on; K2 is the famous one, but K1 is wanted here.
explanation.definitionFit: A ski is a long runner fixed to a boot for travelling over snow.

clue.text: Hero's one for villain — friend to Caesar, J?

blocks.note: Mark Antony was Julius Caesar's ally
Caesar, J gives Julius as a surname then initial; in the same style the friend is Antony, M for Mark

explanation.surface: A hero is the opposite of a villain, like Caesar's friend in Shakespeare.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma and J mimic a register listing surname then initial, so the friend's initial follows his name.
explanation.definitionFit: An antonym is a word of opposite meaning, as hero is to villain.

clue.text: Competitor for place on river an enterprising sort

indicators.note: in an across clue on means placed after, so the competitor follows the river

blocks.note: the Indus is the great river of Pakistan
a trialist plays in a trial match hoping to win a place in a team

explanation.surface: A rower is trying for a seat in the boat on the river.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' means after, so the competitor follows the river.
explanation.definitionFit: An industrialist runs factories or businesses, someone full of commercial enterprise.

clue.text: Customer exactly right and not coming back?

indicators.note: something coming back travels the opposite way, so the word is read from right to left

blocks.note: off pat means learned exactly
R is the abbreviation for right
no is a word of refusal meaning not, then turned round

explanation.surface: A customer is said to be always right, yet this one is not returning to the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exactly right' reads as one phrase; split it, as exactly and right each give letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A patron is a regular client of a shop, restaurant or business.

clue.text: Trader needs minute with English having tirade about check

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the outburst wraps around the next item

blocks.note: M is the abbreviation for minute
E is the abbreviation for English
a rant is a long angry speech
CH is chess notation for check

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper loses his temper over a cheque, in a minute and in English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Check' suggests a bank cheque or an inspection; here it is the chess term.
explanation.definitionFit: A merchant is someone who buys and sells goods, a trader.

clue.text: Male relative one in semi-religious order?

blocks.note: first meaning: a brother sharing only one parent
second meaning, whimsical: a brother in a religious order who is only half committed

explanation.walkthrough: A monk is addressed as brother, so a member only halfway into a religious order would be half a brother.
explanation.definitionFit: A sibling who shares one parent is a half-brother, and a part-time friar would be half a brother.

clue.text: Persian perhaps shuffled cards, meeting the French in game

indicators.note: shuffling a pack mixes it up, so the letters of the word are mixed

blocks.note: a Persian is a breed of cat
the letters of cards, rearranged
le is French for the

explanation.surface: A Persian man shuffles the cards and joins a French player for a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Persian' reads as a person; it is the long-haired cat breed.
explanation.definitionFit: Cat's cradle is a children's game of making string figures between the fingers.

clue.text: Meat and drink kept as fresh

indicators.note: fresh means new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

blocks.note: rum is a spirit
the letters of kept as, rearranged

explanation.surface: Food and drink are kept fresh.
explanation.definitionFit: Rump steak is a cut of beef from the hindquarters.

clue.text: Racketeer in old film from Massachusetts originally to be buried outside

indicators.note: originally points to how a word begins, so only its opening letter is used
outside says the verb goes around the selected letter

blocks.note: the dead lie in their graves
the opening letter of Massachusetts

explanation.surface: A gangster in a classic movie came from Massachusetts and ends up in the ground.
explanation.walkthrough: Harry Lime is the black-market racketeer played by Orson Welles in The Third Man (1949).
explanation.definitionFit: Harry Lime is the villain of The Third Man, who dealt in diluted penicillin in post-war Vienna.

clue.text: Culminating point: that's getting married in a church

indicators.note: in places the wedding letter within the church abbreviation

blocks.note: taken as written
M is the abbreviation for married
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: The high point of a romance is a wedding in church.
explanation.definitionFit: The acme is the highest point or peak of achievement.

clue.text: Pelt across river, ripping up land?

indicators.note: lying across something means stretching over it, so the coat goes round the river letter
in a down clue up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: an animal's pelt is its coat
R is the abbreviation for river
ripping means first-rate, A1, with 1 read as I

explanation.surface: Someone throws things over a river, tearing up the land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pelt' looks like a verb, to throw at; it is an animal's skin. Ripping is old British slang for excellent.
explanation.definitionFit: Croatia is a country on the Adriatic, so it is a land.

clue.text: Culturally deficient person taking book aboard Central Line?

indicators.note: taking aboard means bringing something inside, like a passenger boarding a train

blocks.note: a central line of seats is the middle row
B is the abbreviation for book

explanation.surface: A philistine reads a book on a London Underground train.
explanation.walkthrough: The Central line is a London Underground route; here it is just a line in the centre, a middle row.
explanation.definitionFit: Middlebrow means of only moderate intellectual or cultural ambition, so it fits a person scorned by highbrows.

clue.text: Look down on river holding drinks up

indicators.note: holding means having within, so the river surrounds the drinks
in a down clue up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: the Dee is a river in Wales, England and Scotland
sips are small drinks

explanation.surface: From a height someone gazes at a river carrying drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: To despise someone is to regard them with contempt, as though beneath you.

clue.text: Incestuous son Opus Dei corrected

indicators.note: something corrected has been altered, so the letters are set in a new order

blocks.note: the letters of these two words, rearranged

explanation.surface: A sinful son is put right by the Catholic organisation Opus Dei.
explanation.walkthrough: Opus Dei is a conservative Roman Catholic organisation, apt for correcting a sinner.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Oedipus unknowingly married his own mother, Jocasta.

clue.text: For questions, do exams

blocks.note: to do someone is to swindle or con them
exams are tests

explanation.surface: A student sits examinations to answer questions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Questions' is a verb here, as in challenging a result.
explanation.definitionFit: To contest a claim is to dispute or question it.

clue.text: Cheap and nasty short containing rum

indicators.note: containing means holding within, so one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: shy of means short of, as in two votes shy
rum is British slang for odd or strange

explanation.surface: A cheap tot of rum served short measure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rum' looks like the drink; it is the adjective meaning peculiar.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoddy goods are badly made and of poor quality.

clue.text: True Grit appropriate for audience?

indicators.note: an audience hears the word, so we want one sounding like the verb rather than spelt like it

blocks.note: to appropriate something is to take it unlawfully

explanation.surface: The film True Grit seems fit for a cinema audience.
explanation.walkthrough: True Grit is a John Wayne western, but here it is plain resolve; 'appropriate' is a verb, not an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Steel means firmness of character, the strength of will also called grit.

clue.text: Criminal let in here to steal order from political official

indicators.note: criminal suggests something crooked, so the letters are bent out of order

blocks.note: the letters of let in here, rearranged
to whip is slang for to steal

explanation.surface: A crook let in here to steal something on the orders of a politician.
explanation.walkthrough: A whip is the party official who makes sure MPs vote; a three-line whip is the most urgent instruction to attend.
explanation.definitionFit: A three-line whip is a strict instruction issued by a party's whip, underlined three times, telling MPs to vote.

clue.text: Boring routine — pity that's not finished!

indicators.note: not finished means stopping short, so the word loses its closing letter

blocks.note: ruth is an old word for pity, as in ruthless

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in a dull routine laments that it never ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A rut is a monotonous habit one is stuck in, like a wheel in a groove.

clue.text: Second-rate skill all right for barman?

blocks.note: B grade is second rate
an art is a skill
OK means all right

explanation.surface: A mediocre talent is good enough for a man who pulls pints.
explanation.walkthrough: Béla Bartók, the Hungarian composer, wrote music measured in bars, hence a 'bar man'.
explanation.definitionFit: A composer deals in musical bars, so the question mark makes Bartók a whimsical man of bars.

clue.text: After fish, do some shopping for marine plant

blocks.note: an eel is a fish
to shop someone is to inform on them, which in British slang is to grass

explanation.surface: After buying fish, someone goes on to shop for seaweed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After fish' puts the fish first; 'shopping' is betraying someone to the police, not buying.
explanation.definitionFit: Eelgrass is a flowering seagrass that grows underwater in shallow coastal seas.
